title: Orthogonal Projections & Gram-Schmidt
summary: Shadows, nearest points, projection matrices, orthonormal bases.

title: Linear Regression
summary: Normal equations, geometry (the fit is a projection!), why more features never raise training error, least squares = Gaussian MLE, gradient descent, Gauss-Markov.
figs: F2.1 | Fit as projection | 3D: y, column space of X, ŷ and residual; drag y.
F2.2 | Adding features | Slider adds columns; residual length only shrinks.
F2.3 | Gaussian noise gives squared loss | Points with vertical Gaussian bumps; switch to Laplace to see absolute loss.
F2.4 | Gradient descent on a bowl | Contours, step-size slider, divergence demo.
F2.5 | Gauss-Markov | Estimate clouds for OLS vs another unbiased estimator.

title: MLE vs MAP, Ridge & Lasso
summary: Priors as regularizers: Gaussian prior gives Ridge, Laplace prior gives Lasso. Bias and variance of Ridge, and why Lasso gives exact zeros.
figs: F3.1 | MLE vs MAP | Likelihood curve times prior curve gives the posterior; slide the prior width and watch the peak move toward zero.
F3.2 | Ridge vs Lasso constraint | Loss ellipses touching a circle (Ridge) versus a diamond (Lasso); drag the unconstrained optimum.
F3.3 | Coefficient paths | A lambda slider shrinks all weights; Lasso weights hit exactly zero, Ridge weights do not.
F3.4 | Shrink vs threshold | One-dimensional plot of the OLS weight against the Ridge and Lasso weights.

title: Bias–Variance Tradeoff & the Eigenvalue View
summary: Test error = bias² + variance + noise; how OLS and Ridge differ in each eigen-direction; why training error is optimistic.
figs: F4.1 | Dartboard | The four bias/variance quadrants; resample training sets and watch the weight estimates scatter around the target.
F4.2 | Many fits, one truth | Draw many training sets, fit a stiff and a wiggly curve to each, and show their average against the true function.
F4.3 | Model complexity curve | A degree slider with training error, test error, and the U-shaped test curve.
F4.4 | Eigen-directions | The ellipse of X^T X with its axes, and the variance of the estimate along each axis.
F4.5 | Ridge per direction | A lambda slider showing bias squared, variance and their sum for a large and a small eigenvalue.
F4.6 | Training vs test error | Error against the ratio p/n for linear regression, showing sigma^2(1-p/n) and sigma^2(1+p/n).

title: Logistic Regression
summary: Why log-odds, the Bernoulli natural parameter, cross-entropy as negative log-likelihood, convexity with no closed form, Newton and IRLS, and the linear decision boundary.
prereq: Ch 2 regression, MLE and gradient descent
figs: F5.1 | Why not a straight line | A straight line and a sigmoid fitted to 0/1 data; add an outlier far to the right and watch the line tilt while the sigmoid barely moves.
F5.2 | Probability, odds, log-odds | A slider for p showing the odds and the log-odds, and the sigmoid curve with the slider point marked.
F5.3 | Cross-entropy loss surface | The convex bowl of the loss over two weights, with the gradient descent path drawn on it.
F5.4 | Gradient descent vs Newton | The same loss, with both optimizers side by side and an iteration counter.
F5.5 | Decision boundary | Draggable points of two classes; the line w^T x = 0 and the probability bands move with the fit.

title: Support Vector Machines
summary: Geometric margin, hard margin and its dual, soft margin as hinge loss, kernels and Mercer's condition, and support vector regression.
figs: F6.1 | Distance to a hyperplane | Drag a point x0 and see its foot point on the line, its signed distance, and the vector w.
F6.2 | Maximum margin | Rotate and shift a separating line; the margin width, support vectors and the value of 1/||w|| update live.
F6.3 | Slack variables and C | A slider for C; margin violators light up with their slack, and the street widens as C shrinks.
F6.4 | Hinge vs logistic loss | The two loss curves against the margin y f(x), with 0-1 loss for reference.
F6.5 | Kernel trick | One-dimensional data that no threshold separates, lifted to 2D with phi(x)=(x, x^2) where a line separates it.
F6.6 | RBF kernel and gamma | Decision boundary and support vectors for several values of gamma.
F6.7 | Support vector regression | A fitted line with an epsilon-tube; points inside cost nothing, points outside get slack arrows.

title: Decision Trees
summary: Entropy, information gain (never negative, by Jensen), Gini impurity, regression trees, why greedy splitting gives high variance, and how bagging and boosting respond.
figs: F7.1 | Entropy and Gini curves | The two impurity measures plotted against the class proportion p; drag p and read both values live.
F7.2 | Split explorer | A one-dimensional data set; click a threshold and see the two child nodes, their entropies and the information gain, with the best threshold marked.
F7.3 | Tree depth vs decision boundary | A two-class data set with a depth slider; the boundary goes from one cut to a jagged fit around single points, with training and test error beside it.
F7.4 | Greedy trap | The XOR data set, where every first split has zero gain; add a noise feature and watch the greedy tree choose it.
F7.5 | Resample the data | Redraw the training set slightly and refit; the top split and the whole tree below it change, showing instability.

title: Bagging & Random Forest
summary: Bootstrap samples, averaging many trees, the variance formula sigma^2[rho + (1-rho)/B], why decorrelating trees matters, and why forests use deep trees.
figs: F8.1 | Bootstrap sampling | Draw a bootstrap sample from a small data set; repeated points are drawn thicker, left-out points are greyed, and a counter shows about 63 percent unique points.
F8.2 | Averaging trees | Fit many trees to bootstrap samples of a noisy curve; show each tree faintly and the average in bold, with B as a slider.
F8.3 | Variance vs B | A curve of the ensemble variance against the number of trees for a slider on rho; it falls and flattens at rho times sigma squared.
F8.4 | Feature subsampling | A data set with one dominant feature; show how often each feature is chosen for the first split with and without a random feature subset m.
F8.5 | Out-of-bag error | A strip of points per tree marked in-bag or out-of-bag, and the out-of-bag error curve settling as trees are added.

title: Gradient Boosting
summary: Gradient descent in the space of functions: each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss. Residuals for squared error, y minus p for logistic loss, shrinkage, and bias reduction.
figs: F9.1 | Boosting round by round | A noisy curve with a slider for the number of trees; the fitted function is built up from one small step per round, with the residuals shown as vertical bars that shrink.
F9.2 | Residual equals negative gradient | The squared-error loss for one point as a function of the prediction F, with the slope marked at the current F and the residual drawn beside it.
F9.3 | Parameter space vs function space | Two panels: gradient descent moving a weight vector down a bowl, and boosting moving a prediction vector one tree-step at a time.
F9.4 | Learning rate and rounds | Sliders for eta and T; training and test error against T, showing small eta needing more rounds and the test error turning upward at large T.
F9.5 | Classification version | Two-class points with the boundary after each round, and the pseudo-residual y minus p drawn at each point as an arrow.

title: AdaBoost
summary: Exponential loss, the sample-weight view, the optimal vote alpha = 1/2 ln((1-err)/err), weight updates, the training-error bound, and AdaBoost as gradient boosting with a different loss.
figs: F10.1 | Sample weights round by round | Two-class points drawn with size proportional to weight; after each round the misclassified points grow and the correct ones shrink, and the current stump is drawn.
F10.2 | Vote strength alpha vs error | The curve alpha = 1/2 ln((1-err)/err); a slider on err shows the vote, with alpha reaching 0 at err = 0.5 and turning negative beyond it.
F10.3 | Building the ensemble | The decision boundary of the weighted vote after 1, 2, 3 and more stumps, with each stump's vote strength shown beside it.
F10.4 | Loss functions compared | Exponential, logistic, hinge and 0-1 loss plotted against the margin y F(x), showing the exponential loss exploding for confident mistakes.
F10.5 | Training-error bound | Round-by-round product of 2 sqrt(err(1-err)) against the actual training error, with a slider on the edge gamma.

title: XGBoost
summary: Second-order (Newton) boosting: the regularized objective, optimal leaf weights, the split-gain formula, and why the Hessian acts as a sample weight.
figs: F11.1 | First vs second order | The loss of one point against the prediction F, with the tangent line (first order) and the parabola (second order) at the current F; a slider moves F and shows how far each approximation stays accurate.
F11.2 | Split gain explorer | Points sorted on one feature with their g and h values; click a threshold to see G_L, H_L, G_R, H_R and the gain, with the best threshold marked and a slider for gamma.
F11.3 | Leaf weight and lambda | A leaf with a chosen G and H; a slider for lambda shows the optimal weight -G/(H+lambda) shrinking towards zero.
F11.4 | Gain and pruning | A small tree with the gain of every split written on it; a slider for gamma turns branches grey as their gain drops below zero.
F11.5 | Gradient vs Newton boosting | The same data fitted by first-order boosting and by XGBoost; training error against rounds for both.

title: K-Means
summary: Latent variables and hard cluster labels, the distortion objective, alternating assignment and mean updates, why it always converges (to a local minimum), initialization, and choosing K.
prereq: Basic idea of an unobserved variable
figs: F12.1 | K-Means step by step | Points on a plane with K movable centres; buttons for Assign and Update colour the points and move the centres, with J shown after every half-step.
F12.2 | Same data, different starts | Several random initializations run to convergence, with the final J of each; the best run is highlighted.
F12.3 | Elbow plot | A slider for K showing the clustering beside a curve of J against K, with the bend marked.
F12.4 | Voronoi view | The plane coloured by nearest centre, showing that K-Means boundaries are straight lines halfway between centres.
F12.5 | When K-Means fails | Elongated, unequal-size and ring-shaped clusters where K-Means draws the wrong boundaries, with the true groups shown beside it.

title: Latent Variables & the EM Algorithm
summary: Why a log of a sum blocks a closed form, the E-step (posterior responsibilities) and M-step (expected complete-data log-likelihood), the Jensen's-inequality lower bound, why the likelihood never decreases, and K-Means as hard EM.
prereq: Ch 3 maximum likelihood and Bayes' rule
Ch 7 Jensen's inequality for concave functions
figs: F13.1 | Jensen's inequality | A concave curve (the logarithm) with a chord between two points; a slider moves the weight lambda and shows the chord always below the curve, and the gap shrinking to zero when the two points coincide.

F13.2 | EM as lower-bound climbing | The log-likelihood curve over a parameter, with a lower-bound curve that touches it at the current theta; the E-step draws the bound, the M-step jumps to its peak, and the next bound is drawn there.
F13.3 | Hard vs soft assignment | One point between two clusters; a toggle switches between a one-hot assignment and probabilities, shown as a split colour.

F13.4 | Two coins, step by step | The five sets of flips with the responsibility of each set drawn as a split bar; buttons for the E-step and the M-step update the two estimated biases and the log-likelihood.
F13.5 | Log of a sum vs sum of logs | The complete-data log-likelihood (easy, one clear peak) beside the observed-data log-likelihood (several bumps), for the same model.

title: Gaussian Mixture Models
summary: The mixture density and its one-hot latent variable, responsibilities by Bayes' rule, and the closed-form updates for the means, covariances and mixing weights (with a Lagrange multiplier), all read as the EM steps of Chapter 13.
prereq: Matrix derivatives of log det and quadratic forms
figs: F14.1 | GMM fitting step by step | Two-dimensional points with K ellipses (one per component); E-step and M-step buttons recolour the points by responsibility and move, stretch and rotate the ellipses, with the log-likelihood beside it.
F14.2 | Responsibility colours | Points drawn with a colour blended from the component colours in proportion to gamma; points in the overlap region look mixed.

F14.3 | Update intuition | A single component with its weighted points: the mean is the weighted centre, the covariance is the weighted scatter, and pi is the fraction of total weight, with a slider for how much weight each point carries.
F14.4 | Covariance types | The same data fitted with spherical, diagonal, tied and full covariances, showing the ellipse shapes and the parameter count of each.
F14.5 | Collapse of a component | One component shrinking onto a single data point while its density and the log-likelihood shoot upwards, then the same run with a small added regularizer.
